summary: Recursion is delegation. You handle ONE step yourself (the 'do something' part) and ask a smaller copy of yourself to handle the rest. Get three things right and you're done: (1) the base case that lets the recursion stop, (2) the induction step that shrinks the problem, (3) the return value the caller uses. Everything else — TOH, factorials, palindromes, fast power — is decoration on that triangle.

thoughtProcess.title: 1. Define what the function returns BEFORE writing the body.
thoughtProcess.body: Write the contract first: 'reverse(s, l, r) — true if s[l..r] is a palindrome'. The body almost writes itself. Skip this and you'll mutate the wrong state.

thoughtProcess.title: 2. Identify the base case first.
thoughtProcess.body: Smallest input where you can answer directly without recursing. Forgetting the base = infinite recursion = stack overflow. Two-element vs single-element edge: think twice.

thoughtProcess.title: 3. Trust the recursion (the 'leap of faith').
thoughtProcess.body: Assume the recursive call already works correctly on the smaller input. Now do ONE thing with that result. This is the hardest mental shift — practice with palindrome, factorial, print-array before tackling TOH.

thoughtProcess.title: 4. State threading vs return values.
thoughtProcess.body: Two styles: (a) accumulate via a parameter (helper(i, acc) — like fast power passing the running product); (b) return a value and combine (factorial(n) returns n * factorial(n-1)). Don't mix — pick one per function.

thoughtProcess.title: 5. Be aware of stack depth.
thoughtProcess.body: Java's default stack is ~10⁴ frames. Print-1-to-N recursively is fine for N=10⁵ on JVM? No — convert to iteration or accept the StackOverflowError. Tail-recursive style helps reasoning but JVM doesn't optimise it.

thoughtProcess.title: 6. Fast power: halve, don't decrement.
thoughtProcess.body: pow(a, n) = (a^(n/2))^2 (then × a if n is odd). O(log N) instead of O(N). The general 'split in halves' pattern recurs in merge sort, BS, divide-and-conquer.

commonMistakes.title: Forgetting the base case
commonMistakes.wrong: int factorial(int n) { return n * factorial(n - 1); }
commonMistakes.right: int factorial(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return n * factorial(n - 1); }
commonMistakes.why: No base = infinite recursion = StackOverflowError. Always start with the base.

commonMistakes.title: Base case at n == 0 only, missing n == 1
commonMistakes.wrong: boolean isPalindrome(s, l, r) { if (l == r) return true; ... }
commonMistakes.right: boolean isPalindrome(s, l, r) { if (l >= r) return true; ... }
commonMistakes.why: Even-length strings end with l > r, not l == r. Use l >= r for safety.

commonMistakes.title: Fast power without halving
commonMistakes.wrong: long pow(int a, int n) { if (n == 0) return 1; return a * pow(a, n - 1); }
commonMistakes.why: Decrement-by-one is O(N). Halve-and-square is O(log N). For N = 1e9 that's the difference between TLE and instant.

commonMistakes.title: Mutating shared state in recursion without restoring
commonMistakes.wrong:
// 'all indices' problem — pushing to a global list, never popping
List<Integer> result; void rec(int i, int[] A, int B) { if (A[i] == B) result.add(i); rec(i+1, A, B); }
commonMistakes.why: Globals are fine for accumulators (no backtracking needed); but for backtracking problems you MUST undo the change. Add the parameter version if you're not sure.

commonMistakes.title: Tower of Hanoi: wrong auxiliary peg in recursion
commonMistakes.wrong: toh(n - 1, from, to, aux);   // moved top n-1 to destination first
commonMistakes.why: The classic 'move top n-1 OUT OF THE WAY using the target as helper'. Get the parameters wrong → you'll dump disks in the wrong order and crash on a 'big-on-small' check.

commonMistakes.title: Tail-style code expecting JVM tail-call optimisation
commonMistakes.wrong: void print1ToN(int i, int N) { if (i > N) return; System.out.println(i); print1ToN(i + 1, N); }
commonMistakes.right: for (int i = 1; i <= N; i++) System.out.println(i);  // convert to iteration for large N
commonMistakes.why: JVM does NOT do tail-call optimisation. Deep tail-recursive code overflows at ~10⁴ frames. Convert hot recursive functions to loops when N is large.

keyPatterns.name: Factorial / Linear Recurrence
keyPatterns.when: f(n) = n × f(n-1) or any single-arg recurrence with a clean base.

keyPatterns.name: Print Sequence (forward or reverse)
keyPatterns.when: Traverse 1..N or N..1 with side effects.

keyPatterns.name: Palindrome via Two-Pointer Recursion
keyPatterns.when: Symmetric checks where l and r move toward each other.

keyPatterns.name: Tower of Hanoi (classic 3-peg recursion)
keyPatterns.when: Move N disks from source to destination with one auxiliary, larger on bottom.

keyPatterns.name: Index Collector (first / last / all)
keyPatterns.when: Walk array recursively, append matches to a result list (or short-circuit on first hit).

keyPatterns.name: Fast Power (binary exponentiation)
keyPatterns.when: Compute a^N mod M in O(log N).

edgeCases: n = 0 in factorial → return 1 (not n × factorial(n-1) which would give 0).
Empty string in palindrome → return true (l >= r at the start).
TOH with n = 0 → no moves, return empty list (don't print 'move disk 0').
Fast power: a = 0, n = 0 conventionally returns 1; a = 0, n > 0 returns 0.
Last-index recursion with all matches — must NOT short-circuit on first hit during unwinding.
Print 1-to-N for N = 0 → print nothing (base case triggers immediately).
Index collector when array is empty → res stays empty, no NPE.
Fast power modulus = 1 → every result is 0; the 1 % mod guard handles it.
Mod with negative intermediate (subtraction inside power-of-modular-inverse problems): apply ((x % mod) + mod) % mod.
